failure_summary.description: Clue starts with a pronoun ('They were once called Saratoga Chips after the town...'). The agent answered with the town named in the clue ('Saratoga Springs') instead of what 'They' refers to (potato chips).
A verbatim archive line gave the answer as the bare surname ('| Genet.'), but the agent expanded it to 'Jean Genet'. Rule 3 says to copy the archived form.
The agent kept the branch qualifier the clue already stated ('at Superior') and answered 'University of Wisconsin-Superior'. The key is the parent institution, 'University of Wisconsin'.

The agent picked a mayor because the passage title matched the generic role ('mayor of Washington, D.C.'), ignoring the distinctive event in the clue (2-week sabbatical). It also used the encyclopedia headline name form with a nickname in quotes.

patch.reasoning: Three of the four failures are answer-form or referent errors: the wrong entity, expanding past the archived surname, and keeping a qualifier the clue supplied. The fourth is a person chosen from the role alone, not the distinctive event. The edits are compact and each covers a pattern likely to recur: pronoun-subject clues, person-name form, branch/campus qualifiers, and role-plus-event person clues.

edits.target: - 'One of these <role/title>' ('the 14th one of these spiritual leaders') asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content: - Pronoun-subject clues ('They were once called "Saratoga Chips" after the town where they were first made', 'It was nicknamed X', 'He/She ...'): the answer is what the pronoun stands for, i.e. the thing that bore the quoted name or did the action ('Potato chips'). The place, person or date inside the explanatory clause ('the town ... where they were made') is only an anchor. Never answer with it ('Saratoga Springs'). When the pronoun is 'they/these', the answer is usually a plural or mass-noun category.

edits.target: Still apply the person-name rule above.
edits.content: - Person-name form: (a) if a verbatim archive line gives a bare surname or short form ('... of "The Maids" | Genet.'), the answer is exactly that ('Genet'), not an expanded 'Jean Genet'. Copy the archived form, even when it is shorter than a full name. (b) Without a verbatim hit, give the plain 'First Last' form a trivia key would list. Never use the encyclopedia headline form with middle names, suffixes or a nickname in quotes ('Marion Barry', not 'Marion Shepilov Barry, Jr.'; 'Tony Williams', not 'Anthony Allen "Tony" Williams').

edits.target: Never cut a part that identifies the person: keep the regnal numeral of a king or of a play's title character ('Richard III', not 'Richard'; 'Henry V').
edits.content: - Branch/campus/location qualifiers: when the clue itself supplies the campus, city or branch ('this state university at Superior, not Madison'), strike it from the answer name and give the parent institution or organisation: 'University of Wisconsin', not 'University of Wisconsin-Superior'. This is the delete-clue-words test applied to hyphenated or suffixed qualifiers.

edits.target: Do not choose one that fits only some.
edits.content: - Role-plus-event person clues ('His 2-week sabbatical as mayor of Washington, D.C. made headlines'): the distinctive event or trait identifies the person. The role is shared by many holders. Do NOT choose a person just because a passage title matches the role ('mayor of Washington, D.C.'), or because he is the best-documented or most recent holder. Check which candidate the passages tie to the event. If no passage does, use your own knowledge of who is famous for that episode, and prefer a candidate whose own page is among the retrieved passages and fits the era.
